item.title: [NYT World] Pope Endures Grueling Travel in South America Weeks After Surgery
item.description:
AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTYou have a preview view of this article while we are checking your access. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load.
Flying with Pope Leo XIV over the Andes, halfway through the pontiff’s 12-day trip to South America, the journalists traveling at the back of the plane suspected something was amiss.
They had expected the pope to come out from behind the business-class curtain and take questions, as he had on previous papal flights. Instead, Vatican officials abruptly told the press corps that the pope would not be speaking with them on the nearly five-hour flight from Argentina to Peru.
Was the pope, who had been diagnosed with lung cancer less than a month earlier, feeling ill? Was he too exhausted to talk? Was he taking a nap?
“It’s evident he’s well,” said Maria Montserrat Alvarado, who heads the Vatican’s communications department, when asked why the pope wasn’t taking questions. “He’s running circles around us.”
It was perhaps inevitable that Leo’s every action on this journey, so soon after surgery to remove a lobe of his right lung, would be scrutinized for signs of fatigue or illness, particularly as the Vatican is not known for its transparency.
The three-country trip, which began in Uruguay and concludes in Peru on Monday, involves a grueling schedule of 12 flights, two helicopter rides, nine Masses, 36 speeches and numerous meetings with local bishops and community members.

item.title: [NYT World] Five European Countries Plan to Deport Migrants to Rwanda
item.description:
AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTYou have a preview view of this article while we are checking your access. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load.
Five European countries announced a plan on Monday that would send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda, an experiment that comes as governments across the continent toughen their stances on migration.
The joint push from Germany, Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece was pitched as a way to handle migrants who had no right to stay in Europe but who, for one reason or another, could not or would not return to their home countries.
The project, which is not yet finalized, shows how European leaders’ stance on migration has hardened since the arrivals of 2015-16, when countries like Germany admitted more than a million asylum seekers. With far-right groups like the Alternative for Germany rising in popularity, centrist leaders have gradually taken a less welcoming stance.
“For me, today marks a crucial step toward a new migration system,” Mette Frederiksen, the prime minister of Denmark, said at a news conference on Monday.
The pilot project is expected to start on a small scale, with perhaps 100 or 200 deportees. Critics are already worried both about the idea of sending people to a nation to which they have no connection, and about the risk that human rights will not be sufficiently protected in Rwanda.
Why Rwanda?
The country has a history of courting migration-related deals.
Britain developed a plan to send asylum seekers there in 2022, though judges in London ultimately ruled the effort unlawful and it was later abandoned. The United States has recently deported people to Rwanda.

Pakistan's imprisoned ex-leader Imran Khan appeals for urgent medical care
Imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan has appealed to Pakistan's top judges for urgent medical treatment for himself and his wifeByMUNIR AHMED Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 9:10 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
ISLAMABAD -- Pakistan’s imprisoned former Prime Minister Imran Khan appealed Monday to the country’s top judges, seeking their help in getting urgent medical treatment for himself and his wife and alleging that authorities had failed to implement an earlier court order to transfer him to a hospital in the capital, Islamabad.
In an open letter and conveyed to the judges through his lawyer, Khan said his blood pressure had risen sharply and that doctors had warned him he was at risk of a brain hemorrhage and cardiac arrest.
According to the letter released to the media by Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf party and lawyer Salman Safdar, the former premier said that his wife, Bushra Bibi, also needed further eye surgery and could permanently lose her sight without it.
Khan has been in prison since 2023 after being convicted in a graft case. He was removed from office in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022. Despite his legal troubles, Khan remains a central and popular figure in Pakistan, and the PTI wants his release.
Khan's wife is also serving a prison term on graft charges.
Tariq Fazal Chaudhry, a Cabinet minister, disputed Khan’s account, saying he was receiving regular medical care and accusing him of seeking political advantage. In a post on X, Chaudhry said Khan has been taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad eight times for examinations, where his health and blood pressure were found to be satisfactory.

item.title: [CBS News World] U.K. mulls changing sexual consent laws after Russell Brand case
item.description:
London — Britain's government is considering changing the U.K.'s laws on the legal age of sexual consent as a woman who claims she was raped by convicted sex offender Russell Brand campaigns to criminalize sex between adults and 16- or 17-year-olds.
British Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said over the weekend that "appalling" stories of "abuse of power by powerful men" had emerged last week, warranting consideration of a new law that would set out different ages of consent depending on the ages of the individuals involved.
Already practiced by several other nations, the merits of this staggered age of consent approach have "been raised and will be discussed" by the government, McFadden said, adding that he "can't tell you what the conclusion of that would be, but the last week has certainly put that up in lights."
A day after Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault, fellow British television personality and author David Walliams was named as the subject of multiple allegations of grooming young girls and harassing female colleagues.
British comedian and actor Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court in London on Nov. 5, 2026.
Zeynep Demir/Anadolu via Getty Images
Under current U.K. law, an adult of any age can have sex with a consenting person 16 years old or older. If a staggered system were imposed, it could make it illegal for anyone 18 or older, for instance, to have sex with individuals aged between 16 and 18, regardless of whether they gave verbal consent.

item.title: [NYT World] Airstrikes on Iran Missile Sites May Shed Light on Justification for Dams
item.description:
AdvertisementSKIP ADVERTISEMENTYou have a preview view of this article while we are checking your access. When we have confirmed access, the full article content will load.
Environmentalists have long been mystified by the significant proliferation of dams and water transfer projects like pipelines and tunnels across Iran, especially in regions that had no apparent need for them.
Some analysts think they now know the answer after U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on concealed Iranian missile sites this year targeted many of the same areas. These analysts have concluded that the water projects may have been developed to support the country’s military buildup.
Given the secrecy surrounding Iran’s missile program, any connection between it and Iran’s ambitious, decades-old initiative to develop water infrastructure remains speculative. But some experts find the evidence highly suggestive.
Nima Shokri, an expert on water security, and his team at the Hamburg University of Technology, in Germany, had for years tracked an unusually high number of dams across Iran — at least 533 of them, among the most of any country in the region.
“It was always puzzling to me,” he said. “Why were they building so many dams?”
In the spring, Dr. Shokri was perusing news about the war in his home country when he came across a map plotting airstrikes that had targeted suspected military sites. The pattern — a semicircle of dots from north to south — nearly matched that of his own map marking the locations of dams.
His old question, he said, was superseded by a new one: “Why does it seem that wherever we have dams, there is a missile strike close by?”

item.description:
Mexican drug kingpin Félix Gallardo, founder of Guadalajara cartel, dies at 80
Gallardo, nicknamed the “Boss of Bosses,” died of multiple organ failure.ByThe Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 12:01 PM
MEXICO CITY -- Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, a former drug lord considered one of the godfathers of Mexico’s drug trafficking industry and a founder of the notorious Guadalajara cartel, died at a hospital in the western city of the same name. He was 80.
Félix Gallardo, nicknamed the “Boss of Bosses,” died Sunday at 2 p.m. of multiple organ failure, the Jalisco state security department said in a statement.
The notorious drug kingpin had been hospitalized since Friday after being rushed from the Puente Grande prison, where he had been held since 1989. He was serving a combined 77-year prison sentence for drug trafficking offenses and the 1985 killing of U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena.
Along with Rafael Caro Quintero and Ernesto Fonseca Carrillo, Félix Gallardo founded the Guadalajara cartel, which dominated drug trafficking in Mexico during the 1980s and eventually splintered into several criminal organizations in the country’s north, including the Sinaloa cartel.
Caro Quintero was released on procedural grounds in 2013 but recaptured in July 2022. He was extradited to the United States in February 2025 along with 28 other prisoners wanted by U.S. authorities on drug-related charges.
All three cartel founders were convicted in Mexico in connection with Camarena’s killing. The DEA agent was kidnapped and tortured before his body was found in 1985.

Huang resigned as boss of the AI chip giant last week after the emergence of two affairs, one of which was with a woman suspected of spying for China and another allegedly with one of his employees.

The pair were among more than 175,000 signatories of an open letter calling for the board to reinstate Huang while an ongoing internal probe is conducted.

"I guess maybe one lesson is more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that," he told reporters as he left the White House.
The president's comments come after the "Stand with Jensen" campaign group, which claims to be made up of current and former Nvidia employees, partners, shareholders and supporters, demanded the return of the former chief executive.
They expressed concerns the ex-Nvidia boss "was removed without meaningful due process".
Huang had been expected to weather the storm following the revelation of an affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy.

Pope bids 'hasta luego' to his second homeland of Peru as he wraps up marathon South American trip
Pope Leo XIV has bid farewell to his beloved homeland of PeruByNICOLE WINFIELD Associated Press, ASTRID SUÁREZ Associated Press, and LUIS ANDRES HENAO Associated PressNovember 16, 2026, 9:43 AM
Share
LIMA, Peru -- LIMA, Peru (AP) — Pope Leo XIV bid farewell to his beloved second homeland of Peru on Monday with an “hasta luego,” after a marathon 12-day South American tour that tested his stamina after lung cancer surgery.
During the traditional popemobile ride before Leo's final Mass, someone threw an apparent rosary toward the pope that seemed to hit him in the face. The pope winced and touched his temple, but he proceeded on and the Mass began as planned. The Vatican said some 1.5 million people attended.
The faithful often toss rosaries, stuffed animals, sports jerseys and other items towards the popemobile and Leo has often wowed the crowd with his quick reflexes in catching them. His bodyguards, though, have lamented that such tossed objects are among their chief concerns in protecting the pope when he is out in public.
For the Chicago-born Leo, who spent two decades in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop, the trip was an emotional homecoming to a place that he has credited with teaching him how to be a shepherd. Upon arrival, he declared that Peru was his “patria” or homeland, and he sang the national anthem alongside President Keiko Fujimori. Leo has American and Peruvian citizenship.
“It was here that you taught me how to be a bishop, and this time I learned a little more about serving as the Successor of Peter,” Leo said at the end of Mass.
Over the course of the trip, it became clear that Leo modeled his ministry in Peru and now for the universal Catholic Church on the figure of the first archbishop of Lima, St. Turibius of Mogrovejo.

item.title: [BBC World] Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
item.description:
Image source, ReutersByOlivia Ireland and Bethany Bell, Reporting fromViennaPublished16 November 2026, 11:17 GMTUpdated 1 hour ago
Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.
Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.
The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.
Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.
The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024.
Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".
The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.
The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.
In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.
In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".

Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.
The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.
In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.
Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.
In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.

Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they are redeploying troops to defend the country's interim capital, Aden, following weeks of intensified fighting with the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
The Southern Armed Forces said it was withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the southern end of the Red Sea, to reinforce positions around Aden and neighbouring areas.
Houthi-run media say the movement has taken control of the evacuated territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.
The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the key shipping route which the Houthis seized in a surprise offensive in September.
Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis. The Iran-backed fighters said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.
But the Saudi-backed Southern Armed Forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority".
It said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area" with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats".
"This step is driven by the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and neighbouring governorates, reinforcing the front lines and addressing existing threats."

One of the AI industry's most important figures has resigned amid allegations that he had extramarital affairs with two women - one a suspected Chinese spy and the other a company executive.
Chip-maker Nvidia hired a major law firm earlier this week to investigate CEO Jensen Huang's reported relationship with a woman who was allegedly a Chinese intelligence asset.
Now he has resigned after its stocks plummeted on Wednesday following US media reports about a second alleged affair.
Huang admitted, external earlier this week to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and he apologised for hurting her and their children.
Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters.
Nvidia stocks plummet in US after CEO Jensen Huang quits in wake of affair with suspected Chinese spy
How was Huang removed?
Nvidia's board met on Wednesday evening to decide whether its CEO should remain with the company.
It had 11 directors on its board, including Huang. The firm's CEO could be removed with or without cause by a majority vote of directors.
But that wasn't in the end needed - the board instead announced Huang had resigned as president, CEO and board member.
It thanked him for his "immeasurable contributions" to Nvidia, which it said were "profound".
There was no mention of the accusations of adultery.
Who will replace him?
Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO.
It is less clear is who will replace Huang on a permanent basis.

Watch: Chris Cash says counter-terror officers entered his bedroom and arrested himByJoe Pike, politics investigations correspondent and Phil Kemp, politics reporterPublished11 November 2026
A British man who was charged with spying for China has told the BBC he was a "convenient fall guy" for UK police and security services who wanted to put espionage threats by foreign states "on the map".
Chris Cash, a former parliamentary researcher, has shared more than 6,000 messages with us revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK - including the 2022 Tory leadership battle to decide the next prime minister.
The messages show how Cash's friend in China, Chris Berry - with whom he had been sharing information - dramatically described a "secret" meeting between Berry and a high-ranking Chinese official.
Berry said he had been told that China was concerned about how a British MP it had sanctioned might be promoted to a cabinet role.
The messages also reveal how Cash used his friend as a reference during vetting for a parliamentary pass - which was approved.
Like Cash, Berry was also charged with espionage. The two men consistently maintained their innocence.
In Cash's first interview since his acquittal, which sparked a political row over the government's failure to designate China as a "threat", he says he would "never do anything" to harm UK national security.
But he admits he was "unprofessional and naive" to send "gossiping" texts to his friend, whom he met in 2018 when they both taught English in a school in China.
Although the trove of messages shows him discussing sensitive topics, there is no evidence in them that Cash was paid by, or sympathetic to, the Chinese Communist Party.
